title: Smell-O-Vision
hook: A 1960 mystery film sent smells to every seat through tubes on cue.
peek: Scent of Mystery promised a film you could smell, with scents piped to each cinema seat at key moments in the plot. It became one of the best-known flops in film history, and a rival system beat it to the screen by weeks.
lede: Smell-O-Vision was the work of the Swiss-born inventor Hans Laube, backed by the producer Mike Todd Jr. For the 1960 film Scent of Mystery, cinemas were fitted with a machine that released about 30 different scents through a network of tubes running to the seats. Each smell was triggered by a cue on the film, so the audience would smell what was happening on screen.

bullets.text: Laube's machine was nicknamed the smell brain. It held the scents in a row of containers and released them as the film reached each cue, with perfumes for things like pipe tobacco, bread and the sea.

At early screenings the vents made an audible hiss, and some smells arrived a few seconds after their scene. People in the balcony complained the scents were faint, and audiences were seen sniffing loudly to catch them.
A rival system called AromaRama opened weeks earlier, at the end of 1959, with a travel film about China. It pushed scents through the cinema's air-conditioning, and reviewers made fun of both.
Scent of Mystery did not earn back its cost. It was later cut down and sent back out without the smells under a new name, Holiday in Spain, and Smell-O-Vision was never used again.
